subsystems.name: Deep drilling system
subsystems.role: bore a 10–20 km hole into hot crystalline basement rock, where conventional bits wear out within metres.
parts: gas or mist circulation to lift vaporised rock
conventional rotary rig for the upper hole

subsystems.name: Well construction
subsystems.role: keep the hole open and sealed against 400 °C rock and corrosive brine.
parts: thermally stable cement or metal-to-rock seals

subsystems.name: Reservoir or loop
subsystems.role: create the surface area across which heat moves from rock to fluid.
parts: or a sealed closed loop with a return path

subsystems.name: Working fluid circuit
subsystems.role: carry heat from depth to the surface.
parts: supercritical water or carbon dioxide as working fluid

subsystems.name: Surface power plant
subsystems.role: convert the delivered heat into electricity and useful heat.

subsystems.name: Monitoring and control
subsystems.role: track temperature, flow, fluid loss and any induced seismicity.
parts: downhole fibre-optic temperature and strain sensing

buildSteps.title: Find the heat
buildSteps.detail: Magnetotelluric and seismic surveys, plus slim temperature-gradient holes, map how deep the 400 °C isotherm sits. Below a few kilometres the imaging is poor, so the first deep hole is always a gamble.

buildSteps.title: Drill the upper hole conventionally
buildSteps.detail: Rotary bits and drilling mud take the well to roughly 4–6 km, casing and cementing in stages as it goes.

buildSteps.title: Switch to energy drilling in the basement
buildSteps.detail: Below the depth where bits fail, a millimetre-wave or plasma head melts and vaporises rock instead of grinding it; a gas or mist stream lifts the glassy cuttings out. The deepest borehole yet, over 12 km, was drilled for science with conventional bits and took years.

buildSteps.title: Complete the deep section
buildSteps.detail: High-temperature casing is run and either left open-hole or fitted with a perforated liner, using seals that survive 400 °C.

buildSteps.title: Create the heat exchanger
buildSteps.detail: Either inject fluid at high pressure to shear existing fractures across a large rock volume, or seal the hole so it becomes a closed loop with a coaxial or U-shaped return path.

buildSteps.title: Drill the return wells
buildSteps.detail: One or more further wells are drilled at a set distance so fluid can travel through hot rock and come back hot.

buildSteps.title: Test circulation
buildSteps.detail: Fluid is pumped for weeks to months while produced temperature, flow rate, fluid loss and seismic response are measured.

buildSteps.title: Build the surface plant
buildSteps.detail: Heat exchangers feed a supercritical or binary turbine; surplus heat can be piped to industry instead.

buildSteps.title: Operate and monitor
buildSteps.detail: The plant runs for decades while operators watch for thermal short-circuiting, mineral scaling and slow creep of casing in hot rock.

prerequisites.why: demonstrated in laboratories and shallow field tests, but not yet through kilometres of hard rock.

prerequisites.tech: Enhanced geothermal stimulation of crystalline rock
prerequisites.why: commercial enhanced geothermal systems are being deployed in hot rock at moderate depth, giving a playbook that has not yet been tested at supercritical temperatures.
most sensors, tools and elastomers fail above roughly 250–300 °C, well short of the target.
supercritical fluids dissolve and re-precipitate minerals aggressively and corrode ordinary steels.
existing well materials degrade quickly when held at 400 °C for years.
fossil plants already run at comparable temperatures and pressures, so surface conversion is proven once heat can be delivered.

pathway.milestone: enhanced geothermal systems at 3–5 km are moving from research sites to early commercial projects
pathway.unlocks: a repeatable method for drilling and stimulating hot rock, though each well produces modest power.

pathway.milestone: field trials of millimetre-wave and plasma drilling through hard basement rock at pilot scale
pathway.unlocks: a drilling method that does not wear out, which is the key that unlocks depth.

pathway.milestone: a first circulated supercritical well pair, deeper than 6 km and held above 400 °C for months
pathway.unlocks: real data on fluid chemistry, casing survival and how much power one well can deliver. Iceland's deep drilling project reached supercritical conditions in a well a few kilometres deep, but it was never turned into a producer.

pathway.milestone: a multi-well pilot plant selling power and heat commercially
pathway.unlocks: a cost curve for ultra-deep drilling, the way offshore wind and shale drilling both drove their own costs down.

pathway.milestone: replication at volcanic and basement sites worldwide
pathway.unlocks: firm, weather-independent baseload power and industrial heat in many more places than conventional geothermal allows.
